videoIdeas.title: The 3 questions that make people remember you
videoIdeas.hook: Stop asking people 'so what do you do?' — it's why nobody remembers you.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart01's networking-questions video did 2.1M views and the cold-email one did 180k — practical, save-worthy 'here's exactly what to say' content is the single biggest format working in this niche right now, and you have nothing like it. This is your public speaking pillar made actionable.
videoIdeas.script: Stop asking people 'so what do you do?' It's a dead question and it's why nobody remembers you after the event. Here's what to ask instead. One: 'What's keeping you busy at the moment?' — it lets them talk about what they actually care about, not their job title. Two: 'How did you get into that?' — people love telling their origin story, and you learn how they think. Three: 'Who should I be talking to that I'm not?' — now they're working for you. Notice none of these are about you. That's the point. People don't remember the person who impressed them. They remember the person who made them feel interesting. Be that person.

visuals.setting: Standing, smart-casual, filmed in a hallway or event-style space — blazer or shirt, natural light, slight handheld energy like you're walking out of a room. Mid energy, conversational, not shouty.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'STOP SAYING THIS' over you physically crossing out the words 'so what do you do?' with your hand, then the three questions appear one by one as bold on-screen captions as you say them.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-handshake, then freeze-frame and 'this is the moment most people blow it'
On-screen text punchline first: 'The question that gets you forgotten' then cut to you
Count-up overlay 1/2/3 pinned on screen so people know it's save-worthy

videoIdeas.title: If you're in your 20s, learn to speak before you learn to code
videoIdeas.hook: Nobody's going to promote the smartest person in the room. They'll promote the one who can explain it.
videoIdeas.rationale: doctordaanish's 'if you're in your 20s pls save this' series is a repeatable, high-save format (60k+ views across parts). You can own the public-speaking angle of it — a gap none of your competitors are filling specifically.
videoIdeas.script: Nobody's going to promote the smartest person in the room. They'll promote the one who can explain it. If you're in your 20s, here's what nobody tells you. Your technical skill gets you in the door. Your ability to speak decides how far you go. You can be the best in your field and still get talked over by someone with half your knowledge and twice your clarity. That's not fair. It's just true. So learn to hold a room. Learn to pause instead of filling silence with 'um'. Learn to say the point first and the explanation second. Record yourself and watch it back — yeah it's painful, do it anyway. Being well-spoken isn't a personality you're born with. It's a skill you drill. Start now while the stakes are low.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing in a clean, slightly professional setting — desk, bookshelf, or plain wall. Shirt, calm older-brother energy, steady eye contact, minimal movement so the words carry.
visuals.visualHook: Bold on-screen text 'IF YOU'RE IN YOUR 20s — SAVE THIS' top-centre, pinned for the whole video, with a subtle counter so it reads as part of a series.
otherHookIdeas: Open on you mid-sentence, no intro, straight into the claim (cold open)
On-screen text punchline: 'Smartest ≠ promoted' then cut to your face
Flash the word 'um' on screen with a red strike-through when you mention filler words

videoIdeas.title: You can be struggling and still be a leader
videoIdeas.hook: You can lead people and still not have it together yourself. Both are true.
videoIdeas.rationale: lifeofdinoo_'s shortest, most stripped-back post — 'You can pray and still need help. Both can be true.' — hugely outperformed everything (and your own 'in the room' post did well with the same punchy structure). This short, honest, dual-truth format is working. Apply it to leadership/mindset.
videoIdeas.script: You can lead people and still not have it together yourself. Both are true. We've built this idea that a leader is someone who's sorted — calm, certain, five steps ahead. That person doesn't exist. The people you look up to are managing doubt in real time, same as you. The difference is they decided the work mattered more than their comfort. Waiting until you feel ready is just a polite way of never starting. Lead scared if you have to. Just lead.

visuals.setting: Tight, intimate framing — closer to camera than usual, plain background, softer tone. Darker/evening light. Less performance, more like you're telling one person something true.
visuals.visualHook: Black screen, white centred text: 'You can lead and still feel lost.' holds for 1.5 seconds before you appear — mirrors the dinoo minimalist style that's winning.
otherHookIdeas: No music for the first 3 seconds — silence as a pattern interrupt
Single sentence on screen, then it deletes itself word by word
Start on your face already mid-eye-contact, no movement, just the line

videoIdeas.title: What a Muslim general in 711 can teach you about commitment
videoIdeas.hook: He landed his army in enemy territory — then burned every ship behind them.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia post already pulled 1,640 views with zero caption optimisation — history-as-leadership-lesson is a proven lane for you and nobody in your competitor set is doing it. Sharpen the hook and tie it to a modern takeaway.
videoIdeas.script: He landed his army in enemy territory — then burned every ship behind them. 711 AD. Tariq bin Ziyad crosses into Spain, outnumbered, and orders the boats burned. Now there's no retreat. No 'if it doesn't work we'll go home.' The only options are forward or die. And they won. Here's the point, and it's not about war. Most of you aren't failing because you can't do the thing. You're failing because you've left yourself an exit. A backup plan you secretly prefer. A 'we'll see how it goes.' Commitment isn't loud. It's just removing the option to quit. Burn the ships. Then there's only one direction left.

visuals.setting: Standing, confident, plain or textured dark background. Shirt. Firm, deliberate delivery — this one carries weight, so slower pace, strong pauses.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'HE BURNED HIS OWN SHIPS' over a dramatic still/illustration of ships or coastline for the first beat, then cut hard to your face.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on the single word 'RETREAT' with a red X slammed over it
Map/illustration zoom from North Africa into Spain as you set the scene
On-screen date stamp '711 AD' ticking up like a counter for intrigue

videoIdeas.title: Being in the room is the whole game
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest, smartest, or most connected person in most rooms I'm in. Doesn't matter.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'Might not be the fastest but I am in the room' post was your second-best performer (2,675 views, strong like ratio) — the line clearly resonated. Expand that exact thought into a full script; you already know the hook works.
videoIdeas.script: I'm not the fastest, smartest, or most connected person in most rooms I'm in. Doesn't matter. Because I'm in the room. You spend so long thinking you need to be the best before you're allowed to show up. That's backwards. Showing up is what makes you better. The gap between you and the people you admire isn't talent — it's that they kept putting themselves in rooms they felt too small for, over and over, until they didn't anymore. You don't earn your place and then enter. You enter, feel out of place, and earn it from the inside. So stop waiting to be ready. Get in the room. Be the worst one there for a while. That's how it's supposed to feel.

visuals.setting: Film actually walking into a space — a building entrance, a lecture hall, an event. Movement from outside to inside mirrors the message. Smart-casual, energetic but grounded.
visuals.visualHook: Open mid-walk pushing a door open, on-screen text 'be the worst one in the room' — the action matches the message instantly.
otherHookIdeas: Text-first punchline: 'You don't earn the room. You enter it.'
Contrast cut: empty doorway, then you stepping through
Freeze-frame on you mid-step with the hook line pinned

videoIdeas.title: How to stop your voice from shaking when you speak
videoIdeas.hook: Your voice shakes because you're trying to hide that you're nervous. Stop hiding it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Pure practical public-speaking tactics are your strongest untapped pillar and the exact 'here's how to actually do it' format driving birdtart01's reach. You have real authority here via the MCB leadership programme — lean into teaching the skill directly.
videoIdeas.script: Your voice shakes because you're trying to hide that you're nervous. Stop hiding it. The shake comes from tension — you're holding your breath, clenching, performing calm you don't feel. Three fixes. One: breathe out slowly before your first word. Empty lungs can't support a shaky voice. Two: slow down. Nervous people rush because they want it over with. Deliberate pace signals control to your body, not just the audience. Three: accept the nerves instead of fighting them. Nobody confident-looking actually feels nothing — they've just stopped treating nerves as a problem. The goal was never to not be nervous. It's to be nervous and say it well anyway.

visuals.setting: Clean, well-lit, standing or seated at a slight angle — teaching energy. Shirt. Calm, measured delivery that itself demonstrates the slow-pace tip.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '1 reason your voice shakes' with a subtle visual of a waveform/trembling line that steadies as you talk.
otherHookIdeas: Demonstrate a deliberately shaky nervous voice for 2 seconds, then cut to your normal steady voice — pattern interrupt
Text punchline: 'The goal was never to feel calm' as the opener

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your top post at 6,252 views — far above your average. The hook is a direct question ('What do you do on the MCB Visionary Leadership Programme?') which pulls in people curious about leadership opportunities, and it ties to a real, credible institution. This is proof your leadership pillar has the most pull.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption reads like a programme brochure, not you. 10 comments on 6k views is low engagement for the reach — the post informs but doesn't provoke a response. Rewrite the caption in your voice with a question that demands a reply ('Most of you will never apply to something like this. Why?') to convert views into comments.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your best-written line and the numbers back it — 122 likes and 12 comments on 2,675 views is a strong ratio. Short, punchy, dual-truth structure that's exactly the format winning across the niche right now. This is your voice at its sharpest.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the idea on the table as a caption instead of making it the spine of a full video script. The hashtags (#running #halfmarathoner) pull a fitness crowd, not your self-development audience. Rebuild this line into a mindset reel (see the 'in the room' idea) and drop the generic sport hashtags.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: The history-as-leadership-lesson angle is a genuine gap none of your competitors occupy, and the Tariq bin Ziyad hook ('In 711 AD, Christians were begging Muslims to come and liberate them') is instantly intriguing. 1,640 views with zero caption optimisation shows the format has legs.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 0 comments and only 33 likes means the story informed but gave no takeaway people could apply to themselves. The caption front-loads the date and context instead of the drama. Lead with the sharpest image (burning the ships) and always land the modern lesson so people have a reason to engage, not just admire.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Opening on a shared pain point — 'Burnout affects so many of us, whether you're a medical student or not' — is a good relatable hook that speaks directly to your audience's reality, and the burnout/mental-health topic overlaps with what's performing for dinoo and daanish.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 701 views is one of your weakest, and it reads as a promo for the Sabr app rather than value from you. Audiences scroll past content that feels like an ad. Give the burnout insight for free first — your actual take on spotting it early — and let the app be a soft mention at the end, not the whole point.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes is your highest like-count anywhere — conviction content with a clear moral stance and a hadith clearly resonates with your Muslim audience. The Prophetic quote on changing injustice gives the post weight and shareability that your lighter posts don't have.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (carousel) with no view count and only 1 comment, so despite the likes it didn't spark discussion or reach. This belongs as a video — you speaking to camera with that conviction would travel far further. Convert high-stance written posts like this into talking-head reels and end with a question that invites people to speak out too.
